methodology: Ranges are built from scope-matched local observations and shown with Price Confidence: INSUFFICIENT under 10 observations, DIRECTIONAL at 10-24, PUBLISHED (median with P25-P75) at 25+, and HIGH only at 50+ with a strong share of written quotes and final invoices and no single provider dominating the sample. We report medians and percentiles, not averages, and we never blend advertised, quoted, and final-invoiced prices. Current ranges are built from Austin operators' published pricing (advertised rates) and are being upgraded with written quotes and final invoices. We show the confidence because we'd rather be honest about uncertainty than pretend to a precision we haven't earned yet.

faqs.q: Is $150–$350 a month reasonable for weekly pool service in Austin?
faqs.a: That's the fair local range across Austin operators' published rates. Basic productized plans start near $99–$189; full weekly service with chemicals typically runs $225–$385 depending on pool size and complexity. Always confirm what's included before comparing quotes.

This range is built from Austin operators' advertised prices — a solid starting signal, but advertised rates aren't the same as what people actually pay. As we add written quotes and final invoices, the range tightens and confidence rises.

faqs.q: Does weekly service include equipment repair?
faqs.a: Almost never. Routine service covers cleaning and water chemistry. Pumps, heaters, and filter repairs are billed separately, usually at an hourly rate plus parts. Ask for that rate up front.

pool_projects.name: Pool Remodeling
pool_projects.head: pool remodeling austin
pool_projects.intro: A pool remodel can mean anything from a fresh interior finish to a full transformation with new tile, coping, decking, and equipment. Because scope varies so widely, so does price — which is exactly why comparing quotes on the headline number misleads.
cost_drivers: Scope: resurface-only vs. full remodel with tile, coping, and decking
Interior finish: plaster (low) vs. quartz vs. pebble (high)
Decking square footage and material (concrete, pavers, travertine)
Equipment upgrades (variable-speed pump, heater, automation, saltwater)
options: New interior finish. Roughly $7,000–$13,000 for a standard pool.
Adds waterline tile and coping. Often $12,000–$25,000.
Finish, tile, coping, decking, and equipment. $25,000–$60,000+.
questions: Is this a resurface only or a full remodel — and what's in each line item?
What interior finish is quoted, and what's its warranty and lifespan?
Are decking, tile, and coping included or separate?
Are equipment upgrades (pump, heater, automation) in scope?
faqs: How much does it cost to remodel a pool in Austin?

It depends heavily on scope. A resurface-only refresh runs roughly $7,000–$13,000; adding tile and coping pushes toward $12,000–$25,000; a full remodel with decking and equipment can run $25,000–$60,000+. Define the scope first, then compare quotes line by line.
Pool remodel vs. resurface — what's the difference?

Resurfacing replaces just the interior finish. A remodel is broader — it can include tile, coping, decking, equipment, and new features. If your shell is sound and you just want it to look and feel new, resurfacing may be all you need.
How long does a pool remodel take?
A resurface is often about a week; a full remodel with decking and equipment can run several weeks depending on scope and weather.

pool_projects.name: Pool Resurfacing
pool_projects.head: pool resurfacing austin
pool_projects.intro: Resurfacing replaces your pool's interior finish — plaster, quartz, or pebble. It's the most common pool project, and the finish you choose drives most of the cost and how long it lasts.
options: Lowest cost (~$4–$8/sq ft). Typically lasts about 7–10 years.
Mid-range (~$5–$10/sq ft). More durable and stain-resistant.
questions: What finish is quoted — plaster, quartz, or pebble — and the price difference?
Is tile and coping repair included or extra?
What warranty comes with the finish, and who honors it?
Is water for the refill included?
faqs: How much does pool resurfacing cost in Austin?
Roughly $7,400–$13,000 for a standard pool, depending on finish. Plaster is cheapest; quartz and pebble cost more but last longer.
How often does a pool need resurfacing?
Plaster typically every 7–10 years; quartz and pebble last longer. A rough or stained surface, or plaster showing through, is a sign it's time.
Is $10,000 a fair price to resurface a pool?
It can be, for a mid-size pool with a quartz or pebble finish and some tile work. Compare scope, not just price — upload the quote and we'll show how it stacks up.

pool_projects.head: pool repair austin
pool_projects.intro: Most pool repairs are equipment — pumps, filters, heaters, and plumbing. Costs range from a simple part to a full equipment replacement, so the diagnostic and an itemized quote matter.
cost_drivers: What failed: pump, filter, heater, plumbing, or automation
signs: Pump won't prime or is making noise
Water loss beyond normal evaporation (possible leak)
questions: What's the diagnostic/service-call fee, and is it applied to the repair?
Is this a repair or a replacement, and why?
What's the hourly rate and the part cost, itemized?
What warranty covers the parts and labor?
faqs: How much does pool repair cost in Austin?

Simple repairs (seals, O-rings, timers) start around $150; a pump or filter service runs a few hundred; a full pump or heater replacement can run $700–$5,500+ depending on type. Ask for the diagnostic fee and itemized parts plus labor.
Should I repair or replace pool equipment?

If a pump is more than about 8–10 years old, or the repair is more than half the replacement cost, replacing it (with an efficient variable-speed pump) often pays off in energy savings. Ask your pro to compare both.

faqs: How much does pool leak detection cost in Austin?
A leak-detection service typically runs $300–$600 depending on method and complexity; the repair is usually quoted separately. Some companies apply the detection fee to the repair — ask.
How do I know if my pool is leaking?

Try the bucket test: mark the water line, fill a bucket to the same level, and compare after 24 hours. If the pool drops noticeably more than the bucket, you likely have a leak rather than just evaporation.
